questions.question: What does it mean for $f\colon X\to Y$ to be injective?
options: Different elements of $X$ map to different elements of $Y$
Every element of $Y$ must be hit
Every input maps to the same output
The domain and codomain must be equal, universally and without exception.
questions.explanation: Injective means distinct inputs give distinct outputs: $x_1\neq x_2\Rightarrow f(x_1)\neq f(x_2)$.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted
option_explanations: Every element of $Y$ being hit is surjectivity, not injectivity.
All inputs sharing one output is the opposite of injective (a constant map).
Injectivity says nothing about the domain equalling the codomain.

questions.question: Which implication is used for injectivity?
questions.explanation: Injectivity is the implication $x\neq y\Rightarrow f(x)\neq f(y)$: different inputs cannot collide.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted; Quality round 2: direct definition wording and duplicate-stem differentiation
option_explanations: $x=y\Rightarrow f(x)\neq f(y)$ is false for any function, since equal inputs give equal outputs.
$f(x)=f(y)\Rightarrow x\neq y$ is backwards and self-contradictory.
$x\neq y\Rightarrow f(x)=f(y)$ forces collisions, the opposite of injective.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Which example is injective on $\mathbb{R}$?
questions.explanation: $x^3$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$, so different inputs give different outputs: injective.

option_explanations: $f(x)=0$ is constant; every input shares the output $0$.
$f(x)=1$ is constant; all inputs map to $1$.

questions.question: Which example is not injective on $\mathbb{R}$?
questions.explanation: $x^2$ is not injective on $\mathbb{R}$: $(-2)^2=2^2$, so distinct inputs share an output.

$f(x)=x$ is the identity, clearly injective.
$f(x)=x+1$ is strictly increasing, hence injective.

questions.question: If $f(x) = f(y)$ for two different inputs $x\ \neq y$, what conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: Two distinct inputs with the same output form a collision, which is exactly the failure of injectivity.

option_explanations: A collision is the opposite of injective.
$x,y$ are given as inputs, so they lie in the domain.
The specific formula is irrelevant; any colliding function fails injectivity.

questions.question: How can restricting the domain change whether a formula is injective?
options: Changing the domain never affects injectivity
Every polynomial is injective on every domain
A function is injective only if it is constant
questions.explanation: Restricting the domain can remove collisions: $x^2$ is not injective on $\mathbb{R}$ but is injective on $[0,\infty)$.
questions.source_support: Injectivity is a property of the function on its chosen domain.

$x^2$ is a polynomial that fails injectivity on $\mathbb{R}$.
Constant functions are the least injective; injectivity does not require constancy.

questions.question: Why is a strictly increasing function automatically injective?
options: Because its range is all of $\mathbb{R}$
questions.explanation: If $f$ is strictly increasing, $x<y$ implies $f(x)<f(y)$, so distinct inputs never share an output.
questions.source_support: Injectivity forbids two inputs sharing an output.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Strict monotonicity gives injectivity with no continuity assumption.
The range need not be all of $\mathbb{R}$; e.g. $\arctan$ is injective with bounded range.
Boundedness is unrelated; $f(x)=x$ is injective and unbounded.

questions.question: Is a constant function $f(x)=c$ injective on a domain with at least two points?
options: No; many inputs share the output $c$.
questions.explanation: A constant $f(x)=c$ sends every input to $c$, so any two distinct points collide: not injective on a domain with $\ge2$ points.
questions.source_support: Injectivity requires distinct inputs to have distinct outputs.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Constant functions are never injective on a domain with two or more points.
The value of $c$ is irrelevant; the collision happens for every $c$.
Even a two-point domain already produces a collision.

questions.question: Injectivity is a statement about which of these?
options: Whether two different inputs can share an output
Whether every codomain element is attained
Whether the domain equals the codomain
questions.explanation: Injectivity is exactly the question of whether two distinct inputs can map to the same output.
questions.skill_detail: injectivity is about inputs not codomain
questions.source_support: Injective concerns distinctness of outputs for distinct inputs.

option_explanations: Whether every codomain element is attained is surjectivity.
Continuity is a separate analytic property.
Equality of domain and codomain is unrelated to injectivity.

questions.question: Graphically, $f$ is injective when every horizontal line $y=c$ meets the graph:
questions.explanation: Injective means each output value is hit at most once, so every horizontal line meets the graph at most once (horizontal line test).

questions.question: Which implication is equivalent to injectivity when written contrapositively?
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of $x\neq y\Rightarrow f(x)\neq f(y)$ is $f(x)=f(y)\Rightarrow x=y$, the standard injectivity test.

questions.question: If $f$ is injective and you know the value $f(x)$, what can you recover about $x$?
questions.explanation: Injectivity means each output comes from exactly one input, so knowing $f(x)$ pins down $x$ uniquely.
questions.skill_detail: injective lets the input be recovered
questions.source_support: Injective functions map distinct inputs to distinct outputs.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Injectivity gives full recovery of the input, not nothing.
Two possible inputs would be a collision, contradicting injectivity.
You recover the entire input, not merely its sign.

questions.question: For $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb R$, which pair shows non-injectivity?
questions.explanation: $1^2=(-1)^2=1$, so the distinct inputs $1$ and $-1$ share an output: non-injective.

$0^2=0$ and $1^2=1$ differ, so no collision here.
$2^2=4$ and $3^2=9$ differ, so this pair does not show non-injectivity.

questions.question: If $f$ and $g$ are injective and $g\circ f$ is defined, is $g\circ f$ injective?
options: Only if both are also surjective
questions.explanation: A composition of injective functions is injective: $g(f(x_1))=g(f(x_2))$ gives $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ (g inj.), then $x_1=x_2$ (f inj.).

option_explanations: It is always injective in this case, not never.
No relation such as $f=g$ is needed.
